title: The Essay That Stopped Me Skimming
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] By my sixth year of teaching, I'd stopped recognizing the enthusiasm I used to feel walking into my own classroom.
Narrator: Grading had become mechanical, lesson plans recycled without much thought, and I started resenting students for problems that weren't remotely their fault.

Narrator: [carefully] I remember grading an essay so carelessly that I nearly missed a line where a student had written about her father's illness, buried in an otherwise ordinary paragraph about resilience.
Narrator: That line stopped me completely, partly from guilt, realizing how close I'd come to skimming past something a teenager had trusted me enough to write.
Narrator: [reflective] I called her aside the next day, not to discuss grammar, but to ask how she was actually doing, and she looked almost startled that anyone had noticed.
Narrator: That conversation didn't fix my burnout overnight, obviously, exhaustion doesn't dissolve because of one meaningful exchange.
Narrator: [honestly] But it did remind me why I'd chosen this profession in the first place, before the grading and the meetings had buried the reason under logistics.
Narrator: I started, deliberately, reading every essay as though it might contain something worth noticing, even on the nights I was running on no sleep.
Narrator: [gently] Some nights I still fail at that, and I've made peace with the fact that perfection was never a realistic standard to hold myself to.
Narrator: What changed, mostly, is that I stopped treating burnout as a personal failing and started treating it as information, a sign that something in how I worked needed to shift.
Narrator: [calmly] I still get tired, some semesters more than others, but I no longer mistake tiredness for having lost the thing that brought me here.
Narrator: These days, I tell newer teachers that the profession will hollow you out if you let grading replace noticing, and that the noticing was always the actual job.
